Think of match/case as a cookie-cutter test for shapes. You describe what shape you expect — a list with two elements, a dict with a 'type' key, a Point with x > 0 — and Python checks whether your value has that shape. The first matching shape wins, and any named slots in the pattern get filled in automatically.

cards.title: Pattern Types in `match`/`case`
cards.teaser: Python 3.10 defines six core pattern kinds: literal, capture, wildcard, sequence, mapping, and class patterns. Each matches a different structural shape and can nest arbitrarily — a sequence pattern can contain class patterns that contain capture patterns.

The six pattern types are like six different stencils. A literal stencil checks for an exact value. A capture stencil grabs whatever's there and names it. A sequence stencil checks the length and shape of a list. A mapping stencil checks which keys a dict has. A class stencil checks both the type and the field values. Wildcard is the 'anything goes' stencil. You can nest any stencil inside any other.

ExceptionGroup is a bag that holds multiple exceptions at once. When ten tasks fail simultaneously, instead of arbitrarily picking one exception to propagate and silently dropping the other nine, Python puts all ten in a bag and throws the whole bag. You catch the bag and decide what to do with each exception inside it.

Regular except is a bouncer who stops the line when they find someone they recognize. except* is more like a sorting machine: it passes the bag of exceptions through every handler in turn, each one pulling out the exceptions it knows how to handle. Whatever's left at the end gets thrown again.

TaskGroup is a supervisor for a batch of async jobs. You hand it a set of coroutines, it runs them all in parallel, and it waits at the door until every job is done. If any job crashes, the supervisor immediately tells all the other jobs to stop and then hands you a report listing every failure — no crashes swept under the rug.

cards.title: Faster CPython (Python 3.11/3.12)
cards.teaser: The Faster CPython project (Microsoft-backed, PEP 659) made Python 3.11 up to 60% faster than 3.10 on the official benchmark suite, and 3.12 continued the trend. Key techniques: adaptive specialization, cheaper function calls, and a leaner frame object.

runs.text: Python 3.11 delivered a landmark performance improvement through several complementary changes.
(PEP 659) turns hot bytecode instructions into faster, type-specific variants after a few executions — a
on an object whose class never changes becomes a direct slot read rather than a full descriptor lookup.
— whose reference counts are never modified, eliminating cache-line thrashing in multi-threaded programs and in the upcoming per-interpreter GIL work.

blocks have near-zero overhead when no exception is raised (jump-table approach similar to C++).

pyperformance benchmarks show 3.11 is ~25% faster than 3.10 on the geometric mean and up to 60% on specific benchmarks. Real-world gains vary by workload — I/O-bound code benefits less than pure-compute loops.

runs.text: The Faster CPython project is ongoing. Python 3.13 added a JIT compiler (experimental, disabled by default) as the next step. The roadmap targets another significant speedup in Python 3.14+ as the JIT matures.

The CPython interpreter used to look up how to execute every instruction from scratch every time, even if it had done the exact same thing a thousand times before. The Faster CPython project taught it to remember: 'I've seen this attribute lookup on this type before — here's the fast path.' It also stopped allocating heap memory for every function call, which is like keeping a scratch pad on your desk instead of fetching a new notebook from the supply closet each time.

cards.title: `@override` Decorator (Python 3.12+)
cards.teaser: `@typing.override` (PEP 698, Python 3.12+) marks a method as intentionally overriding a parent class method. Type checkers raise an error if the decorated method does not actually override anything — catching silent failures when the parent API changes.

runs.text: A classic refactoring hazard: you rename a method in a base class but forget to rename the override in a subclass. The subclass now has two methods — the old name (orphaned) and the new parent method (unoverridden). This is a silent bug with no error at runtime and no warning from Python itself.

@override is a stamp you put on a method that says 'I am deliberately replacing my parent's version of this.' If your parent later renames or deletes that method, the type checker spots the broken stamp and warns you — because you claimed to be overriding something that no longer exists.

cards.title: Per-Interpreter GIL (PEP 684, Python 3.12+)
cards.teaser: Python 3.12 gave each sub-interpreter its own GIL (PEP 684). Multiple interpreters in the same process can now run Python bytecode in parallel — but sharing objects between them requires explicit marshalling. This is the foundation for GIL-optional Python.

The GIL is like a single token that only one thread can hold at a time to run Python code. Per-interpreter GIL means each isolated Python sandbox gets its own token. Two sandboxes can each have a thread running code simultaneously because they each have their own token — they never compete for the same one. The catch: the sandboxes can barely talk to each other, so you have to pass messages through a narrow channel.

cards.title: Python 3.13 Preview: JIT, Free-Threaded Mode, and Beyond
cards.teaser: Python 3.13 (released October 2024) ships an experimental JIT compiler and an optional free-threaded build (no GIL) as opt-in features. Neither is ready for production, but together they sketch Python's performance roadmap for 2025 and beyond.

runs.text: Other Python 3.13 highlights include an improved REPL with multi-line editing and syntax highlighting, better error messages for common mistakes, and deprecation of some legacy C API functions. The

Neither the JIT nor free-threaded mode is production-ready in Python 3.13. Many C extensions do not yet support the free-threaded build. Evaluate both for Python 3.14 or 3.15 when the ecosystem has had time to adapt. Monitor PEP 703 status and CPython issue tracker for stability reports.

Python 3.13 is putting two experimental engines in the car: a JIT that compiles hot paths to native machine code on the fly, and a mode that removes the GIL lock so threads can genuinely run in parallel. Right now both engines make the car slower under most conditions — they're prototype technology. But they prove the design works, and future versions will tune them until they actually help.
